newsitem.title: SPAIN: ETA in trial of strength with Spanish society.
newsitem.headline: ETA in trial of strength with Spanish society.

text.p: A brazen show of force by ETA rebels in the past month has added to mounting frustration in Spain's northern Basque region and closed the door to a speedy solution to the 29-year separatist conflict.

"ETA has challenged Spanish society to a trial of strength with this escalation of violence," Spain's Interior Minister Jaime Mayor Oreja told reporters after three fatal attacks struck at three areas of Spain in just two days.
The government's staunch refusal to negotiate peace with the separatist rebels, and its increasingly hardline attitude, was the spark for the latest violence.

ETA, which has killed some 800 people in its independence drive, was blamed for a car bomb that killed a military airbase worker in the southern city of Granada on Monday and the fatal shooting of a Supreme Court judge just hours later in Madrid.
On Tuesday, while the funerals for those two victims were held, another supposed ETA gunman killed a businessmen during carnival festivities in the Basque town of Tolosa.
The offensive, the worst in recent memory, is a clear challenge to the nine-month-old conservative government, but far from clear is what ETA (Basque Homeland and Freedom) guerrillas hope to achieve.
The Basques, who are rugged, industrious and fiercely proud of their heritage, were full of hope early in the tenure of Jose Maria Aznar's Popular Party (PP) government.
Aznar led the first right-wing government since the death of fascist dictator Francisco Franco and there were fears he would reinstate Franco's repressive measures against the Basques.
But he showed a surprisingly conciliatory attitude to the Basques and their autonomy drive.
He negotiated parliamentary backing from the nationalist Basque party and appointed an Interior Minister who had grown up in the region and had an intimate grasp of its problems.
Mayor Oreja started to take concrete steps to address some grievances of the radical Basques. He eased the prison policy to move ETA prisoners closer to their families -- a key demand of the rebels.

In addition, the PP was untainted by a 1980s "dirty war" against ETA that killed 28 people and helped end the 13-year rule of the Socialists, who are accused of organising the illegal campaign and trying to cover-up their involvement.
One month after the PP came to power, ETA announced a one-week truce that gripped the nation as a sign of hope that a negotiated end to the violence could be found.
But the conservatives stuck to the Socialist government's policy of refusing talks until ETA renounces violence.
Mayor Oreja is convinced ETA is trying to force the central government to the negotiating table and to give in would play into the hands of the rebels.
"ETA looks at things in terms of war. For them negotiations are not a means to an end, but a symbol of victory," he said.

ETA responded to the government's no-truce no-talk position with a wave of bombings that targeted tourist sites during summer holidays. They shot and killed a Basque businessman and kidnapped another.

Radical youth groups affiliated with the rebels then began to run weekend rampages through Basque towns and cities, firebombing banks, buses and political party centres. They also burned a bookstore that had been a symbol of free expression.
"These supposed saviours of our homeland have lost all human reason and logic," Basque law professor Marc Carrillo says. "They are the authors of continuous violations of human rights."
The intimidation became so oppressive that ordinary Basques are now afraid to speak out against ETA in cafes and bars.
"We have not lived in such a state of tension in the Basque country since the death of Franco," said a Basque journalist.

But when police began to crackdown on the youth groups and to deal heavy blows to ETA's command structure, by making key arrests with the increased help from French police, they were made out to be the oppressors in the eyes of the Basques.
Street violence supporting the separatist cause grew.
It was fuelled last week when an alleged ETA prisoner was found hanged in his cell. The official report said it was suicide but hid the fact that his feet and hands were tied.
The cover-up, which the government later admitted, was a blunder that cost the PP's clean-hands image in the Basque region dearly.
The final straw was when the Supreme Court summoned the entire 25-member leadership of ETA's political wing Herri Batasuna (HB) to answer charges they promoted violence.

Six members were sent to prison after refusing to appear in court last week, three have gone to Belgium to promote their cause and one was found hanged in his family home on Monday in what officials said was a suicide.
"We blame the central government for the atmosphere that is developing as a result of their repressive activities," an HB leader told journalists.
Last week, HB issued a veiled warning that an ETA offensive would be the answer to the Supreme Court's prosecution.
"It could bring costs to society," HB leader Jon Idigoras said. "The actual consequences will not be desired."
